name: Battle of Lake Trasimene
info: Hannibal's Carthaginian army ambushed a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius on the north shore of Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE, during the Second Punic War, and killed or captured nearly all of it.

facts.place: The north shore of Lake Trasimene, south of Cortona, in Etruria (modern Tuscany, Italy); the shoreline has changed since
facts.sides: Rome and its allies under the consul Gaius Flaminius, about 25,000 men in four legions, two Roman and two allied; Carthage and its Gallic, Iberian and African troops under Hannibal, usually assumed to number more than 50,000
facts.outcome: The Roman army was ambushed and nearly all of it was killed or captured; Polybius and Fabius Pictor give 15,000 killed. Rome elected Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator.

t: The Romans were attacked from the flank and rear while marching in column, possibly in poor visibility, and had no chance to form even a rudimentary fighting line.
Of about 25,000 Romans, 15,000 were killed by Polybius's count, and the 6,000 at the head of the column who escaped were surrounded later in the day and surrendered.
Rome answered the defeat by electing Fabius Maximus dictator, who avoided pitched battle; the next year's consuls fought Hannibal at Cannae.
dyk: The destruction of an entire army by an ambush laid by another army is widely considered a unique occurrence; Basil Liddell Hart called it the greatest ambush in history.
ev: Hannibal besieges, captures and sacks Saguntum, and Rome declares war on Carthage
Hannibal defeats the Romans at the Trebia after crossing the Alps
The Carthaginians cross the Apennines by an unguarded route and march into Etruria, plundering
Hannibal ambushes Flaminius's army on the north shore of Lake Trasimene
A few days later the Carthaginians wipe out the cavalry of the second Roman army under Geminus
Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus is elected dictator and adopts a strategy of avoiding pitched battle
Paullus and Varro, elected consuls, offer battle and are defeated at Cannae
Hannibal is defeated at Zama and Carthage agrees to a peace that strips it of most of its territory and power

sections.background:
The First Punic War was fought from 264 to 241 BCE between Carthage and Rome, the two main powers of the western Mediterranean, chiefly over Sicily and its waters, and ended in Carthaginian defeat. Five years later Hamilcar Barca landed in Iberia and turned it into a quasi-monarchical, autonomous territory ruled by the Barcids, which gave Carthage silver mines, agricultural wealth and manpower. Hamilcar ruled as viceroy until 228 BCE, followed by his son-in-law Hasdrubal and then his son Hannibal in 221 BCE. In 219 BCE Hannibal besieged, captured and sacked Saguntum, a city with a treaty of association with Rome, and Rome declared war.

Hannibal marched north from New Carthage in May 218 BCE and crossed the Alps in October, arriving in Cisalpine Gaul with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and an unknown number of the 37 elephants with which he had left Iberia. The consul Publius Scipio was beaten and wounded at the Ticinus. The army of Sempronius Longus, brought north from Sicily, was lured by Numidian cavalry onto ground of Hannibal's choosing at the Trebia, where most of the Romans were killed or captured, though 10,000 under Sempronius fought their way to Placentia.

Rome chose Gnaeus Geminus and Gaius Flaminius as consuls for 217 BCE, recruited further legions, reinforced Sardinia and Sicily, built a fleet of 60 quinqueremes and set up supply depots at Ariminum and Arretium. It fielded twenty-two legions that year, ten more than in 218 BCE.
sections.forces:
The Roman army at Lake Trasimene was Flaminius's, stationed at Arretium: four legions, two Roman and two made up of allies, about 25,000 men in all. A legion traditionally had 4,200 infantry and 300 cavalry, of whom about 1,200 were javelin-armed skirmishers, the velites, and the rest heavy infantry with body armour, a large shield and a short thrusting sword. Allied legions had a larger complement of cavalry. The second Roman army, under Geminus, was on the Adriatic coast, so that the two could block an advance into central Italy.

Carthage usually recruited foreigners. North Africans, often called Libyans, supplied close-order infantry fighting in a tight phalanx, javelin skirmishers and cavalry of two kinds. Iberia and Gaul provided experienced infantry who charged ferociously but had a reputation for breaking off if a fight was protracted, and Balearic slingers were specialists. The numbers are not known. Hannibal fought at the Trebia with 31,000 infantry and 11,000 cavalry, and was then heavily reinforced by local Gauls. It is usually assumed that more than 50,000 fought at Trasimene, and in any event the Carthaginian army was considerably larger than the Roman.

Hannibal chose the ground. The road ran along the north shore and then turned south through a defile, with low hills to the north that came closer to the lake towards the east. The Carthaginians camped, in full view of the Romans, where the hills were closest to the lake. At night he marched his troops behind the hills to the reverse slopes: cavalry furthest west, the north-Italian Gauls to their east and the African and Iberian infantry furthest east, near the camp. Modern historians place most of the light infantry round the defile or reinforcing the Gauls in the centre.
sections.course:
Flaminius, commanding at Arretium, learned that Hannibal had bypassed him and set off in pursuit. Adrian Goldsworthy points out that the army passed through devastated territory and would have felt humiliation, and that landowning officers and small farmers in the legions would have taken the destruction as a provocation. According to Polybius the Romans expected an easy victory, and they followed so fast that they could not reconnoitre properly, closing to less than a day's march behind. On 20 June the Carthaginians passed Cortona and marched along the north shore of the lake.

On the morning of 21 June the Romans set off very early and marched east along the lake, probably in three parallel columns, with a screen of light infantry in front. Flaminius sent out no cavalry scouts for distant reconnaissance, which Roman armies of the time rarely did. Ancient accounts speak of a thick morning mist; some modern historians suggest it was invented or exaggerated to excuse the Romans' unreadiness. The leading Romans met the easternmost Carthaginians and the signal to advance was given, possibly by trumpets. Some ancient accounts say the Romans heard it on their flank and rear but could not see the enemy.

The Romans had no chance to form even a rudimentary line. Some fled, others clustered in groups ready to fight on all sides, and the fugitives and many groups were quickly cut down or captured. In the centre other groups fought hard, and the Gauls suffered heavy casualties before beating them down after three hours. Polybius says Flaminius was surprised and gave no effective leadership; Livy has him active and valiant in trying to rally the army before a Gaul, Ducarius, killed him. Men tried to swim the lake and drowned.
sections.aftermath:
The trap did not close on the 6,000 Romans at the head of the column, possibly those most prepared for battle. They pushed out of the defile against little opposition and marched on. Later in the day Carthaginians under Maharbal surrounded them and they surrendered on a promise of being disarmed and freed, 'with a garment apiece' according to Livy. Hannibal disapproved and applied this only to the allied captives, selling the Romans into slavery. Many Carthaginian infantry, especially Libyans, took captured Roman armour.

The sources are unclear on the fate of the roughly 25,000 Romans engaged. Fabius Pictor has 15,000 killed and 10,000 scattered; Polybius 15,000 killed and most of the rest captured. For Carthaginian losses Polybius gives 1,500 killed, most of them Gauls, and Livy 2,500 killed on the day and many who later died of wounds. A few days later the whole 4,000-strong cavalry of Geminus's army, scouting ahead, was surprised: nearly 2,000 were killed in the first clash and the rest were surrounded and captured next day. Geminus withdrew his infantry to Ariminum.

Roman prisoners were badly treated, but captured Latin allies were treated well and many were freed, in the hope that they would speak well of Carthage and defect. The Carthaginians went on through Etruria and Umbria to the Adriatic, plundering and killing captured adult men, the Gauls especially brutally, and then marched south into Apulia. Rome panicked and elected Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus dictator.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from ancient historians. Polybius, usually reliable, wrote that Flaminius was completely surprised. Livy, openly pro-Roman, wrote two centuries later and otherwise paints a poor picture of Flaminius but has him rally his men. Fabius Pictor, a contemporary annalist and senator, gave a casualty figure. They disagree on what became of the 25,000 Romans, and Polybius and Livy give different Carthaginian losses.

Historians dispute some details. The shoreline has changed since 217 BCE. Some doubt the thick mist reported by ancient accounts. The positions of the Carthaginian light infantry and the Romans' marching order are modern reconstructions. The Carthaginian numbers are not known and can only be approximated.
sections.legacy:
Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes Lake Trasimene as one of the three great military calamities Rome suffered in the first three years of the war, the others being the Trebia and Cannae. Fabius Maximus's strategy of avoiding pitched battle, relying on low-level harassment to wear the invader down while Rome rebuilt its strength, left Hannibal largely free to ravage Apulia for the next year. The Romans then ended the dictatorship and elected the more aggressive Paullus and Varro, who offered battle at Cannae in 216 BCE, where some 70,000 Romans were killed or captured; Richard Miles calls it Rome's greatest military disaster. The Carthaginians campaigned in southern Italy for a further 13 years.

In 204 BCE Publius Cornelius Scipio, the son of the Scipio wounded at the Ticinus, invaded the Carthaginian homeland, defeated the Carthaginians in two major battles and won the allegiance of the Numidian kingdoms. Hannibal was recalled and decisively defeated at Zama in October 202 BCE, and Carthage lost most of its territory and power.

Later military writers have treated Trasimene as exceptional. Basil Liddell Hart wrote that Hannibal planned and executed the greatest ambush in history. Theodore Dodge notes it is the only instance in history of lying in ambush with the whole of a large army, and Robert O'Connell writes that it was the only time an entire large army was effectively swallowed and destroyed by such a manoeuvre.

summary: On 21 June 217 BCE Hannibal ambushed Gaius Flaminius's Roman army of about 25,000 on the north shore of Lake Trasimene, and nearly all of it was killed or captured. Rome elected Fabius Maximus dictator, and the war went on to Cannae and Zama.
references: John F. Lazenby, Hannibal's War: A Military History of the Second Punic War (Aris & Phillips, 1998)
Dexter Hoyos, Mastering the West: Rome and Carthage at War (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Nigel Bagnall, The Punic Wars: Rome, Carthage and the Struggle for the Mediterranean (Pimlico, 1999)
Robert L. O'Connell, The Ghosts of Cannae: Hannibal and the Darkest Hour of the Roman Republic (Random House, 2010)
notes: The article's lead says 15,000 killed and 'nearly all 25,000 killed or captured'; the casualty section gives Fabius Pictor 15,000 killed and 10,000 scattered, Polybius 15,000 killed and most of the rest captured. I give both.

The article's Carthaginian section says that 'in 216 BC' the Carthaginians had 40,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry, not reinforced since crossing the Apennines: the year looks like a slip for 217 BC and the figure is left out.
The lead says Hannibal's army was 'more than 50,000 strong'; the forces section says it is 'usually assumed'. I used the hedged form.

The article says 'thirteen more years' of war after Cannae (lead and aftermath), and the Aftermath says Carthaginians campaigned 13 further years; used as given. Cannae-section says nothing contradicting.
The article says the second army's cavalry were 'wiped out' in the lead but 'nearly 2,000 killed ... the balance captured' in the text; I used the detailed form.
The sources section is short because the article names only Polybius, Livy and Fabius Pictor and the doubts about the mist.
Left out: the fate of Flaminius's attempted rally beyond Livy's version; details of the Roman equipment; the 'Notes', 'Citations' and 'Sources' headings of the article are empty in the saved copy.
